source_text: Sed quoniam nos sermo commonuit de iudicio futuro et de retributione ac suppliciis peecatorum, secundum quod comminantur sanctae scripturae et ecclesiastica praedicatio continet, eo quod iudiei tempore ‘ignis aeternus- et -tenebrae exteriores- et “carcer- et -caminus- et alia his similia peccatoribus praeparata sint, videamus quid etiam de his sentiri. oporteat, Sed ut ad haec competenti ordine veniatur, prius mihi videtur de resurrectione sermo movendus, ut sciamus quid est illud quod vel ad supplieium vel ad requiem ac beatitudinem veniet; de quo et in aliis quidem libris, quos de resurrectione scripsimus, plenius disputavimus et quid nobis de hoc videretur ostendimus. Sed et nune propter consequentiam tractatus pauca inde repetere non videtur absurdum, maxime propter hoe quod offenduntur quidam in ecclesiastica fide, quod velut stulte et penitus insipienter de resurrectione credamus, praecipue haeretici, quibus hoc modo arbitror respondendum. Si confitentur etiam ipsi quia resurrectio sit mortuorum, respondeant nobis: quid est quod mortuum est, nonne corpus? Corporis ergo resurrectio fiet. Tum deinde dicant si utendum putant nobis esse corporibus aut non? Arbitror apostolo Paulo dicente quia “seminatur corpus animale, resurget corpus spiritale”, istos negare non posse quod ‘corpus resurgat vel quia in resurrectione corporibus utamur. Quid ergo? Si certum est quia corporibus nobis utendum sit, et ‘corpora’ ea, quae ceciderunt, ‘resurgere’ praedicantur (non enim proprie resurgere dicitur nisi id, quod ante ceciderit), null dubium est idcirco ea ‘resurgeres, ut his iterum ex resurrectione induamur. Alterum ergo haeret ex altero. Nam et si resurgunt corpora, sine dubio ad indumentum nostri resurgunt, et si necesse est nos esse in corporibus (sieut certe necesse est), non in alüs quam in nostris corporibus esse debemus. Quae si verum est quod resurgunt et :spiritaha- resurgunt, dubium non est quin abiecta corruptione et deposita mortalitate resurgere dicantur a mortuis; ahoquin vanum videbitur et superfluum resurgere quem a mortuis, ut iterum moriatur. Quod ita demum intellegi evidentius potest, si qui diligenter advertat, quae sit -animalis corporis- qualitas, quae in terram seminata ‘spiritalis corporis. reparet qualitatem. Ex -animali- namque “corpore- ipsa virtus resurrectionis et gratia ‘spiritale corpus’ educit, cum id ab -indigmitate- transmutat ad ‘gloriam”. 2. Quoniam ergo haeretici eruditissimi sibi videntur et sapientissimi, interrogabimus eos, si omne corpus schema aliquod habet, id est aliquo habitu deformetur. Et si quidem dixerint esse corpus quod non aliquo habitu deformetur, imperitissimi omnium atque insipientissimi videbuntur. Nullus enim hoc negabit, nisi sit ab omni eruditione penitus alienus. Si vero secundum id, quod consequens est, dixerint quia omne corpus certo quo habitu deformatur, requiremus ab eis, si possunt nobis ‘spiritalis corporis’ habitum demonstrare atque deseribere; quod utique facere nullo modo poterunt. Sed et differentias eorum, qui resurgunt, inquiremus ab eis. Quomodo ostendent verum esse illud, quod dietum est quia “ala caro volucrum, alia piscium; et corpora caelestia et corpora terrestria; sed alia quidem caelestium gloria, alia vero terrestrium, alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarum, stella enim ab stella differt in gloria; ita et resurrectio mortuorum”? Secundum istam ergo consequentiam caelestium corporum ostendant nobis differentias gloriae eorum qui resurgunt, et si ullo genere conati fuerint secundum caelestium corporum differentias aliquam excogitare rationem, quaeremus ab eis, ut etiam secundum terrenorum corporum comparationem differentias resurreetionis adsignent. Nos vero ita intellegimus, quod volens apostolus describere, quanta esset differentia eorum, qui resurgent “in gloria, id est sanctorum, comparationem caelestium corporum sumpsit dicens: “Alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarume. Et iterum volens differentias eorum docere, qui in hae vita non expurgati ad resurrectionem venient, id est peccatores, de terrenis sumit exemplum dicens: “Alia caro volucrum, alia piscium”. Digne etenim sanctis caelestia, terrena peccatoribus comparantur. Haee quidem dicta sint adversum eos, qui “resurrectionem mortuorume, id est resurrectionem corporum negant. 3. Nune vero sermonem convertimus ad nonnullos nostrorum, qui vel pro intelleetus exiguitate vel explanationis inopia valde vilem et abiectum sensum de resurrectione corporis introducunt. (Quos interrogamus, quomodo intellegant ‘animale corpus- gratia resurrectionis immutandum et “spiritale- futurum, et quomodo quod ‘in infirmitate seminatur-. resurrecturum sentiant ‘in virtutes, et quod ‘in ignobilitate-, quomodo -resurgat in gloria; et quod ‘in eorruptione., quomodo ad “neorruptionem- transferatur. Quod utique si credunt apostolo quia corpus ‘in gloria et in virtute et in incorruptibilitate- resurgens, ‘spiritale” iam effectum sit, absurdum videtur et contra apostoli sensum dicere, id rursum ‘carnis et sanguinis- passionibus implicari, cum manifeste dieat apostolus: “Quoniam caro et sanguis regnum dei non possidebunt, neque corruptio incorruptionem possidebit”, Sed et illud quomodo aecipiunt, quod dicit apostolus quia “omnes autem immutabimur”? Quae utique immutatio secundum illum ordinem, quem superius diximus, expectanda est, in qua sine dubio dignum aliquid divina gratia sperare nos convenit; quod futurum credimus hoc ordine quo “nudum granum frumenti aut alicuius ceterorum” in terra seminatum describit apostolus, eui “deus dat corpus prout voluit”, cum prius "granum- ipsum “frumenti- -mortuum fuerit. Ita namque etiam nostra corpora velut “granum- cadere in terram putanda sunt; quibus insita ratio ea, quae substantiam continet corporalem, quamvis emortua fuerint corpora et corrupta atque dispersa, verbo tamen dei ratio illa ipsa, quae semper in substantia corporis salva est, erigat ea de terra et restituat ac reparet, sicut ea virtus, quae inest in grano frumenti, post corruptionem eius ac mortem reparat ac restituit granum in culmi corpus et spicae.- Et ita his quidem, qui regni eaelorum hereditatem consequi merebuntur, ratio illa reparandi corporis, quam supra diximus, dei iussu ex terreno et ‘animali corpore- “corpus- reparat ‘spiritale”, quod habitare possit in caelis; his vero, qui inferioris meriti fuerint vel abiectioris aut etiam ultimi et abstrusi, pro uniuscuiusque vitae atque animae dignitate etiam gloria corporis et dignitas dabitur: ita tamen ut etiam eorum, qui ad ‘ignem aeternum- vel ad ‘supplieia” destinandi sunt, per ipsam resurrectionis permutationem ita corpus incorruptum sit quod resurgit, ut ne suppliciis quidem corrumpi valeat ae dissolvi. 4. Si ergo ita se habet qualitas eius corporis, quod resurget a mortuis, videamus nunc quid sibi velit ‘ignis aeterni- comminatio. 4. Invenimus namque in Esaia propheta designari uniuscuiusque proprium esse ‘ignem’ quo punitur; ait enim: “Ambulate in lumine ignis vestri et in flamma, quam accendistis vobismet ipsis”. Per quos sermones hoc videtur indicari, quod unusquisque peccatorum “flammam-” sibi ipse proprii ‘ignis’ ‘accendat”, et non in aliquem ignem, qui antea lam fuerit accensus ab alio vel ante ipsum substiterit, demergatur. Cuius ignis esca atque materia sunt nostra peccata, quae ab apostolo Paulo ‘ligna et faenum et stipula- nominantur. Et arbitror quod sicut in corpore escae abundantia et qualitas vel quantitas cibi contraria febres generat, et febres diversi vel modi vel temporis secundum eam mensuram, qua intemperies collecta materiam suggesserit ac fomitem febrium (quae materiae qualitas, ex diversa intemperie congregata, causa vel acerbioris morbi vel prolixioris existit): ita anima cum multitudinem malorum operum et abundantiam in se congregaverit peccatorum, conpetenti tempore omnis illa malorum congregatio effervescit ad supplicium atque inflammatur ad poenas; cum etiam mens ipsa vel conscientia per divinam virtutem omnia in memorlam recipiens, quorum in semet signa quaedam ac formas, cum peccaret, expresserat, et singulorum, quae vel foede ac turpiter gesserat vel etiam impie commiserat, historiam quandam scelerum suorum ante oculos videbit expositam: tunc et ipsa conscientia propriis stimulis agitatur atque conpungitur et sui ipsa efficitur accusatrix et testis.
pass_a_gloss: But since our discourse has reminded us of the future judgment and the retribution and punishments of sins, according to what the holy scriptures and ecclesiastical preaching contain, because in the time of judgment 'eternal fire' and 'outer darkness' and 'prison' and 'furnace' and other things similar to these have been prepared for sinners, let us see what ought to be thought about these things. But in order to come to these things in a suitable order, it seems to me that the discourse about resurrection must first be undertaken, so that we may know what it is that comes either to punishment or to rest and beatitude; about which also in other books, which we have written about resurrection, we have discussed more fully and have shown what seems to us about this. But also now, because of the sequence of the treatise, it does not seem absurd to repeat a few things from that, especially because some people are offended in the ecclesiastical faith, because we believe about resurrection in a way that seems to them foolish and utterly foolish, especially heretics, to whom I think we must respond in this way. If they confess that there is a resurrection of the dead, let them answer us: what is it that has died, is it not the body? Therefore, the resurrection of the body will occur. Then let them say whether they think we ought to use bodies or not. I think that when the apostle Paul says that 'the body is sown animal, it will rise spiritual', they cannot deny that the body rises or that we use bodies in the resurrection. What then? If it is certain that we must use bodies, and the bodies that have fallen are said to 'rise' (for it is not properly said to rise except what has previously fallen), there is no doubt that they rise so that we may be clothed with them again after the resurrection. One thing follows from another. For if bodies rise, they rise without doubt for our clothing, and if it is necessary for us to be in bodies (as it is certainly necessary), we ought to be in our own bodies. Which if it is true that they rise and 'spiritual bodies' rise, there is no doubt that they are said to rise from the dead, having cast off corruption and laid aside mortality; otherwise, it will seem vain and superfluous to rise from the dead, only to die again. This can be understood more clearly if someone carefully considers what is the quality of the 'animal body', which, having been sown in the earth, will produce the quality of the 'spiritual body'. For from the 'animal body' itself, the power of resurrection and the grace of the 'spiritual body' bring forth, when it is transformed from 'baseness' to 'glory'. But since the heretics seem to themselves to be very learned and wise, we will ask them if every body has some shape, that is, if it is deformed by some habit. And if they say that there is a body that is not deformed by any habit, they will seem to be utterly unlearned and foolish. For no one will deny this, unless they are completely alien to all learning. But if they say, according to what is consequent, that every body is deformed by some certain habit, we will ask them if they can demonstrate and describe the habit of the 'spiritual body'; which they will certainly not be able to do. But we will also ask them about the differences of those who rise. How will they show that what has been said is true, that 'one is the flesh of birds, another of fish; and there are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies; but one is the glory of the celestial, another of the terrestrial, one is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars, for star differs from star in glory; so also the resurrection of the dead'? Therefore, according to this sequence, let them show us the differences of the glory of those who rise, and if they have tried in any way to devise some reason according to the differences of celestial bodies, we will ask them to assign the differences of the resurrection also according to the comparison of terrestrial bodies. We, however, understand it in this way, that when the apostle wants to describe how great is the difference of those who will rise 'in glory', that is, of the saints, he takes the comparison of celestial bodies, saying: 'One is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars'. And again, when he wants to teach the differences of those who come to the resurrection without being purified in this life, that is, sinners, he takes an example from terrestrial things, saying: 'One is the flesh of birds, another of fish'. For it is fitting that celestial things are compared to the saints, and terrestrial things to sinners. These things, indeed, are said against those who deny the 'resurrection of the dead', that is, the resurrection of bodies. Now, indeed, we turn our discourse to some of our own, who either because of the smallness of their understanding or the poverty of explanation introduce a very vile and abject sense of the resurrection of the body. (We ask them, how they understand the 'animal body' to be changed by the grace of resurrection and to become 'spiritual', and how what is 'sown in weakness' will rise 'in power', and what is 'sown in ignobility' will rise 'in glory', and what is 'sown in corruption' will be transferred 'to incorruption'. Which, indeed, if they believe the apostle, that the body rising 'in glory and in power and in incorruption' has already been made 'spiritual', it seems absurd and contrary to the sense of the apostle to say that it is again entangled in the passions of 'flesh and blood', when the apostle clearly says: 'For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption'. But also, how do they accept what the apostle says, that 'we will all be changed'? Which change, indeed, is to be expected according to that order, which we said above, in which we ought to hope for something worthy of divine grace; which we believe will come to pass in this order, as the apostle describes, when 'a naked grain of wheat or some other thing' is sown in the earth, to which 'God gives a body as he wills', when the 'grain' of wheat itself has first died. So also our bodies are to be thought of as falling to the earth like a 'grain'; in which the reason that contains the bodily substance, although the bodies have died and been corrupted and dispersed, nevertheless, the word of God, that reason itself, which is always preserved in the substance of the body, raises them from the earth and restores and repairs them, just as the power that is in the grain of wheat, after its corruption and death, repairs and restores the grain in the body of the stalk and the ear. And so, indeed, for those who will merit to attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, the reason of repairing the body, which we said above, by the command of God, repairs the 'spiritual body' from the earthly and 'animal body', which can dwell in the heavens; but for those who will be of lower merit or more abject, or even of the last and most hidden, according to the dignity of each one's life and soul, the glory and dignity of the body will also be given: yet in such a way that even for those who are destined for 'eternal fire' or 'punishments', through the very change of the resurrection, the body that rises is incorrupt, so that it cannot be corrupted or dissolved even by punishments. If, therefore, the quality of the body that rises from the dead is such, let us see now what the threat of 'eternal fire' means. For we find in the prophet Isaiah that the 'fire' by which each one is punished is designated as their own; for he says: 'Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled for yourselves'. Through these words, it seems to be indicated that each sinner kindles their own 'flame' of their own 'fire', and does not sink into some fire that has been previously kindled by another or has existed before them. The fuel and material of this fire are our sins, which the apostle Paul calls 'wood and hay and stubble'. And I think that just as in the body, the abundance and quality or quantity of food generate fevers, and fevers of different kinds or times, according to the measure in which the intemperance has collected the material and provided fuel for the fevers (the quality of which material, gathered from diverse intemperance, is the cause of a more bitter or more prolonged disease): so also the soul, when it has gathered a multitude of evil works and an abundance of sins within itself, at the suitable time, all that gathering of evils boils over into punishment and is inflamed into penalties; when also the mind itself or conscience, through divine power, receiving all things into memory, of which it has impressed certain signs and forms upon itself when it sinned, and the history of its own crimes, which it has committed either foully or impiously, will see exposed before its eyes: then also the conscience itself is stirred and pricked by its own goads and becomes its own accuser and witness.

pass_b_english: Our discourse has reminded us of the future judgment and the retribution and punishments of sins, just as the holy scriptures threaten and ecclesiastical preaching contains. Because in the time of judgment 'eternal fire' and 'outer darkness' and 'prison' and 'furnace' and other things like these have been prepared for sinners, let us see what ought to be thought about these things as well. But in order to reach these matters in a fitting order, it seems to me that we must first take up the discourse about the resurrection, so that we may know what it is that will come either to punishment or to rest and beatitude. We have discussed this more fully in other books which we wrote on the resurrection, and there we have shown what seemed right to us. Yet even now, because of the sequence of this treatise, it does not seem absurd to repeat a few points from that work. This is especially so because some take offense at the ecclesiastical faith, judging our belief about the resurrection to be foolish and utterly senseless; chief among them are heretics, to whom I think we must respond in this way. If they confess that there is a resurrection of the dead, let them answer us: what is it that has died, if not the body? Therefore the resurrection of the body will take place. Then let them say whether they think we ought to use bodies or not. When the apostle Paul says, 'the body is sown animal, it will rise spiritual' (1 Cor 15:44), I think they cannot deny that the body rises or that we shall use bodies in the resurrection. What then? If it is certain that we must use bodies, and the bodies that have fallen are said to 'rise' (for nothing is properly said to rise except what has previously fallen), there is no doubt that they rise so that we may be clothed with them again after the resurrection. One thing follows from another. For if bodies rise, they rise without doubt for our clothing; and if it is necessary for us to be in bodies (as it certainly is), we ought to be in our own bodies. If it is true that they rise and that 'spiritual bodies' rise, there is no doubt that they are said to rise from the dead after casting off corruption and laying aside mortality; otherwise it would seem vain and superfluous to rise from the dead only to die again. This can be understood more clearly if someone carefully considers what is the quality of the 'animal body' which, having been sown in the earth, will produce the quality of the 'spiritual body' (1 Cor 15:42-49). For from the 'animal body' itself the power of resurrection and the grace of the 'spiritual body' bring forth the latter, when it is transformed from 'baseness' to 'glory'.

Now since the heretics consider themselves very learned and very wise, we will ask them whether every body has some shape — that is, whether it is formed by some habit. And if they say that there is a body not formed by any habit, they will appear the most unlearned and foolish of all; for no one will deny this unless they are completely alien to all learning. But if, according to what follows, they say that every body is certainly formed by some habit, we will ask them whether they can demonstrate and describe the habit of the 'spiritual body' — which they certainly will not be able to do. We will also ask them about the differences among those who rise. How will they show to be true what has been said: 'one is the flesh of birds, another of fish; and there are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies; but one is the glory of the celestial, another of the terrestrial, one is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars, for star differs from star in glory; so also the resurrection of the dead' (1 Cor 15:39-42)? According to this sequence, then, let them show us the differences of glory among those who rise, and if they have tried in any way to devise some rationale according to the differences of celestial bodies, we will ask them to assign the differences of the resurrection also by comparison with terrestrial bodies. We, however, understand it this way: when the apostle wants to describe how great is the difference of those who will rise 'in glory,' that is, of the saints, he takes the comparison of celestial bodies, saying: 'One is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars.' And again, when he wants to teach the differences of those who come to the resurrection without being purified in this life — that is, sinners — he takes an example from terrestrial things, saying: 'One is the flesh of birds, another of fish.' For it is fitting that celestial things are compared to the saints, and terrestrial things to sinners. These things, indeed, are said against those who deny the 'resurrection of the dead,' that is, the resurrection of bodies.

Now we turn our discourse to some of our own people, who either because of the smallness of their understanding or the poverty of explanation introduce a very vile and abject sense of the resurrection of the body. We ask them: how do they understand the 'animal body' to be changed by the grace of the resurrection and to become 'spiritual,' and how what is 'sown in weakness' will rise 'in power,' and what is 'sown in ignobility' will rise 'in glory,' and what is 'sown in corruption' will be transferred 'to incorruption' (1 Cor 15:42-44)? Which, indeed, if they believe the apostle that the body rising 'in glory and in power and in incorruption' has already been made 'spiritual,' it seems absurd and contrary to the apostle's sense to say that it is again entangled in the passions of 'flesh and blood,' when the apostle clearly says: 'For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption' (1 Cor 15:50). But also, how do they accept what the apostle says, that 'we will all be changed' (1 Cor 15:51)? Which change, indeed, is to be expected according to that order which we spoke of above, in which we ought to hope for something worthy of divine grace; which we believe will come to pass in this order, as the apostle describes when 'a naked grain of wheat or some other thing' is sown in the earth, to which 'God gives a body as he wills,' when the 'grain' of wheat itself has first died (1 Cor 15:37-38). So also our bodies are to be thought of as falling to the earth like a 'grain'; in which the reason that contains the bodily substance, although the bodies have died and been corrupted and dispersed, nevertheless, the word of God — that reason itself, which is always preserved in the substance of the body — raises them from the earth and restores and repairs them, just as the power that is in the grain of wheat, after its corruption and death, repairs and restores the grain in the body of the stalk and the ear. And so, indeed, for those who will merit to attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, the reason of repairing the body, which we said above, by the command of God, repairs the 'spiritual body' from the earthly and 'animal body,' which can dwell in the heavens; but for those who will be of lower merit or more abject, or even of the last and most hidden, according to the dignity of each one's life and soul, the glory and dignity of the body will also be given: yet in such a way that even for those who are destined for 'eternal fire' or 'punishments,' through the very change of the resurrection, the body that rises is incorrupt, so that it cannot be corrupted or dissolved even by punishments.

If, therefore, the quality of the body that rises from the dead is such, let us see now what the threat of 'eternal fire' means. For we find in the prophet Isaiah that the 'fire' by which each one is punished is designated as their own; for he says: 'Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled for yourselves' (Is 50:11). Through these words, it seems to be indicated that each sinner kindles their own 'flame' of their own 'fire,' and does not sink into some fire that has been previously kindled by another or has existed before them. The fuel and material of this fire are our sins, which the apostle Paul calls 'wood and hay and stubble' (1 Cor 3:12). And I think that just as in the body, the abundance and quality or quantity of food generates fevers, and fevers of different kinds or times, according to the measure in which the intemperance has collected the material and provided fuel for the fevers (the quality of which material, gathered from diverse intemperance, is the cause of a more bitter or more prolonged disease): so also the soul, when it has gathered a multitude of evil works and an abundance of sins within itself, at the suitable time all that gathering of evils boils over into punishment and is inflamed into penalties; when also the mind itself or conscience, through divine power, receiving all things into memory, of which it has impressed certain signs and forms upon itself when it sinned, and the history of its own crimes, which it has committed either foully or impiously, will see exposed before its eyes: then also the conscience itself is stirred and pricked by its own goads and becomes its own accuser and witness.
